newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-SMALL-TOWN HEROES LEAVE MARK ON ITALIAN SEASON.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SMALL-TOWN HEROES LEAVE MARK ON ITALIAN SEASON.

text.p: The "Old Lady" stashed away her 24th Italian league title but despite the triumph of wealthy Juventus the 1997 serie A season which ended on Sunday was marked by poor relations proving a point.
Juventus clinched the title nine days before the end of the season and also won the European supercup and world clubs' cup and reached the European Cup final for a fine haul in their centenary year.
Yet the Turin team and other traditional powers of the Italian game had a far from vintage year as several smaller clubs made the most of their limited budgets.

Vicenza and Napoli, two clubs on the brink of financial collapse in recent years, battled in the Italian Cup final with Vicenza winning their first trophy in 95 years to clinch their second-ever appearance in Europe next season.
Udinese -- a provincial side with a tight grip on the purse strings -- finished fifth to make sure of their first appearance in a European club competition since they were founded 101 years ago.
Both Vicenza and Udinese beat Juventus in the league, Udinese 3-0 winners in Turin with only 10 men.
Juventus, who were at times in a class of their own in European competition, were also held 0-0 by serie C part-timers Nocerina in the third round of the Italian Cup.
The honours of top serie A goalscorer meanwhile went to Filippo Inzaghi of Bergamo's Atalanta.
Juve surrendered their European Cup title to Germany's Borussia Dortmund, who became continental champions for the first time, and the league battle was no pushover.
Second-placed Parma, who qualified for the Champions' League despite having never won the title, won more matches than Juventus in a frustrating season.
They were hovering around the relegation zone in November, with coach Carlo Ancelotti heading the list of coaches most likely to face the chop before Christmas.

In the end Juve's two-point margin of victory was the narrowest in Italy since Napoli beat Milan to the "Scudetto" (little shield) in 1990 and the closest for Juventus since they pipped Roma by two points in 1984.
Juventus did not score more goals than other teams -- they ranked only fourth equal in the overall tally -- but they did have the most consistency and by far the best defence.
Parma and Juventus are two of the wealthiest clubs in Italian soccer but ironically Juventus bought fewer players than most rivals before the season started.
They sold off Gianluca Vialli to Chelsea, Fabrizio Ravanelli to Middlesbrough and Paolo Sousa to Dortmund.
The big name import was Frenchman Zinedine Zidane, while Croat Alen Boksic was signed from Lazio.
The true big spenders were Internazionale, whose season was rewarded only with third place in the league and a UEFA Cup final lost to little-known Germans Schalke.
Inter's millions could not buy success and, despite leading the season at one point, they were unsettled to such an extent that English coach Roy Hodgson walked out.
Roma and Fiorentina also turned in dismal performances while outgoing champions Milan finished in 11th place.

That was Milan's lowest serie A finish since they were relegated in 1982 and left the club that has won four league titles since 1992 and three European Cups since 1988 out of European competition next season.
"Finally it's over," declared a banner at the San Siro stadium on Sunday as Milan lost 1-0 to Cagliari.
It probably referred to the disastrous season but it might equally have pointed to the end of an era of success.
Next season, Milan will be a different entity and Sunday was also a day of farewells for familiar names.

Coach Arrigo Sacchi looks sure to leave, with former boss Fabio Capello returning from Spain's Real Madrid, while veteran defender Mauro Tassotti hung up his boots after 17 consecutive seasons to become the youth team coach.
Veteran libero Franco Baresi may well also have played his last game, although he has yet to say so.
The fans exhorted him to stay throughout Sunday's match, hanging a giant banner declaring "Stay with us".
Another banner said "Thanks anyway, Arrigo".
There was no such affection during the season for the legion of foreign coaches who almost became extinct in serie A.
From the seven foreigners who started out, only Sampdoria's Swede Sven-Goran Eriksson made it to the finish and he is leaving the club for a new challenge at Lazio.
Soccer in Italy can be tough for newcomers. Brazilian striker Ronaldo, who may be playing for Inter next season if his transfer from Barcelona goes through, should beware.
